# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

Build the ask call. Ensure unique ids. Evidence paths relative: "src/server.ts", "PLAN.md".

Round structure: one ask call with 7 questions. Each needs label + tradeoff; recommended is index; brief needs where/what/how. Working directory /tmp/askmore-grill.

content.text:
Repo facts gathered: `server.ts` 401s anything without `x-customer-id` (header presence is the only gate — no auth in this code), `GET /orders` also hits Postgres via unbounded `select *`, runtime is Bun, 3 round-robin instances, shared Redis 7 **cluster** (Lua there needs same-hash-slot keys).

Design tree mapped. Round 1 = the frontier: endpoint scope, key, algorithm, counter store, tier mechanism + ownership, rejection shape, one fact only you have (enterprise burst size). Deferred to later rounds until these settle: fail-open/fail-closed (depends on counter store), rollout + shadow mode + notification (depends on tiers, rejection shape, burst fact), exact `Retry-After` semantics.

questions.question: PLAN.md calls POST expensive, but GET /orders also hits Postgres — listOrders is an unbounded `select *` per customer, and customers today poll it. Do we set separate budgets on both endpoints (generous GET, tight POST)?

brief.where: src/server.ts:10-16 — both routes reach Postgres; src/orders.ts:16-18 — listOrders does an unbounded per-customer SELECT *.
brief.what: Which endpoint classes get budgets, and whether there is one or two counters per customer. Not answerable from code: whether GET flood is a risk you accept.
brief.how: Separate budgets: two token buckets per customer, both keys under one `{customerId}` hash slot. POST-only: read path stays unprotected — a GET flood becomes next week's incident.

options.label: Both endpoints, separate budgets
options.tradeoff: Two buckets per customer; protects Postgres from read floods too.
options.description: Generous GET limit, tight POST limit
options.holds_when: listOrders' unbounded SELECT makes GET a real Postgres cost.
options.cost: 2 Redis keys + 2 bucket configs per customer

options.label: POST only
options.tradeoff: Simplest; GET floods still reach Postgres unthrottled.

options.label: One shared budget
options.tradeoff: One counter; normal GET polling eats the customer's POST headroom — wrong shape for enterprise scripts.

questions.question: Every request reaching the handler already carries x-customer-id (missing → 401, cheap, never touches Postgres). Do we key the limit on x-customer-id alone? One aside to correct if wrong: nothing in this code authenticates the header — if callers can forge it today, they can already insert orders for any customer, and rate limiting won't fix that. Is there an authn layer upstream?

brief.where: src/server.ts:7-8 — presence check only, no authn. PLAN.md:14.
brief.what: Key granularity and whether IP adds protection. Depends on whether the header is trusted, which only you know.
brief.how: Customer-only: exact per-customer fairness. Customer+IP: needs the round-robin LB to actually forward real client IP — if it doesn't, IP buckets group whole customer offices.

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Exact per-customer fairness; unauthenticated 401 floods stay unlimited but never reach Postgres.
options.description: Header is authenticated upstream (or trust it for now)
options.holds_when: All handler traffic has an ID anyway; 401 path is a no-op check.

options.label: Customer and IP
options.tradeoff: Catches ID-rotating floods; doubles state, and is wrong unless the LB forwards real client IPs.

options.label: IP only
options.tradeoff: Punishes shared-office customers; pointless since the ID is required on every call.

questions.question: You have 20 enterprise customers who legitimately burst. Fixed window double-allows at boundaries and punishes exactly those bursty-but-fine clients; sliding-window-log is precise but stores per-request timestamps. Token bucket with per-customer refill rate + burst capacity matches 'legitimate bursts' natively. Token bucket?

brief.where: PLAN.md:15; PLAN.md:10 says enterprise integrations legitimately burst.
brief.what: Which counter math; decides burst behavior, Redis cost per request, and what Retry-After can even mean.
brief.how: Token bucket: one atomic Lua eval per request, burst = bucket capacity, tunable per customer. Fixed window: cheapest to write, but boundary bursts of 2×N will break enterprise scripts on the hour.

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Native burst allowance, continuous refill, one Redis round-trip per check; needs Lua in cluster with hash-tagged keys.
options.holds_when: Burst-friendly behavior is a requirement, not a nice-to-have.

options.label: Sliding window counter
options.tradeoff: Approximate, two INCRs, no real burst semantics.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest code; 2× at boundaries and throttles legitimate bursts.

questions.question: With 3 round-robin instances, in-memory counters mean each instance grants the full allowance → effective global limit up to 3× config, and dividing by 3 under-throttles any customer whose traffic skews to one instance. Do we keep buckets in the existing shared Redis, keys hash-tagged like `rl:{customerId}` so the Lua is cluster-legal, with a dedicated `rl:` prefix and short TTLs? And have you actually asked the session-store team whether you may write there?

brief.where: PLAN.md:7-8 — Redis 7 cluster, round-robin across 3 instances; it belongs to another service (sessions).
brief.what: Global correctness vs zero-dependency fuzziness, and blast-radius ownership of a shared cluster. A rate-limiter evicting session keys would be worse than the original incident.
brief.how: Redis: exact global limits, and this choice makes 'what if Redis is down' a live question next round. Memory: no new failure mode on the hot path, limits stay fuzzy within ~3×.

options.label: Shared Redis, hash-tagged
options.tradeoff: Exact global limits; adds Redis to every request's hot path and shares a cluster with sessions — needs the owning team's OK.
options.holds_when: Session team agrees to the extra load and an eviction-policy check.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.tradeoff: No network hop, no new failure mode; global limit fuzzy up to 3×, per-customer tuning divides by 3.

options.label: New dedicated Redis
options.tradeoff: Clean ownership and blast radius; procurement/may not fit 'this week'.

questions.question: For the 20 enterprise customers: per-customer overrides — a small Postgres table (or same-source config) read into cache at startup, numbers owned by support/CS, changed via ticket — rather than a uniform 'enterprise multiplier' or an SRE-edited config file? And confirm: is support/CS actually the right owner of those numbers, or you?

brief.where: PLAN.md:10, PLAN.md:18 — higher limits and ownership both undecided.
brief.what: Override granularity, storage mechanism, and who signs off on numbers. Ownership is organizational; code can't answer it.
brief.how: Per-customer overrides absorb the spread between a 10/s script and a 60/s script; a uniform multiplier mis-sizes most of them. Ownership decides whether limit changes need a deploy or a ticket.

options.label: Per-customer overrides, CS-owned
options.tradeoff: Precise, no deploys to adjust; requires an approval path so numbers don't drift per-request.

options.label: Uniform enterprise tier
options.tradeoff: One number, shippable today; over-provisions some, breaks others.

options.label: Config file, SRE-owned
options.tradeoff: No new table; every adjustment is a redeploy of all 3 instances.

questions.question: What does a rejected request return: 429 with Retry-After (seconds), the draft RateLimit limit/remaining/reset headers, and a JSON body like `{"error":"rate_limited"}` — or a bare 429?

brief.where: PLAN.md:19; server.ts currently returns Response.json for success, plain text for errors.
brief.what: The public contract. Enterprise scripts may treat non-2xx as hard failure, or busy-retry a bare 429 and make Postgres load worse than the original incident.
brief.how: Retry-After + RateLimit headers let well-behaved scripts back off automatically. Bare 429 assumes their retry logic copes — unverified. If you know any enterprise client crashes on 429, say so now.

options.label: 429 + Retry-After + RateLimit headers
options.tradeoff: Auto-backoff for good clients, debuggable; tiny extra work.
options.holds_when: You can't audit 20 integrations' 429 handling before Friday.

options.label: Bare 429
options.tradeoff: Minimal surface; busy-retry loops likely, amplifying load.

options.label: 429 + Retry-After only
options.tradeoff: Backoff without exposing quota numbers you haven't finalized.

questions.question: One number only you has: what peak legitimate orders/second does the biggest enterprise integration actually hit today? The offender did ~67/s. If nobody knows, is your answer 'pick generous defaults and measure in shadow mode before enforcing'?

brief.where: PLAN.md:3 — incident at 40,000 orders/10 min ≈ 67/s; PLAN.md:10 — enterprise bursts unquantified.
brief.what: The default rate/burst numbers, or whether we must measure first. No log access here; only you or shadow mode can answer.
brief.how: Known peak → defaults sized ~2× above it, enforce sooner. Unknown → limits start in shadow mode (count, don't reject) purely to collect this fact; that pushes shadow mode into the rollout round.

options.label: Unknown — measure in shadow
options.tradeoff: Correct numbers eventually; enforcement slips by the shadow window (days).
